name: Zoe Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take calls and chats about missing orders for a garden-supply company called Fieldgate. I find where a delivery stopped, ring the depot, and explain to the customer when plants will actually arrive. The little AI draft is useful for a plain address correction, but I check the stock record myself before I send it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like turning an angry call into a sensible plan for the next delivery. I've done this sort of work for years since secondary school and earn more than a new agent, but I don't run the team. My partner Arun and I still pay a mortgage, and our grown daughters have places of their own.

say: I would welcome **quicker address fixes** while checking delivery dates myself.
I would keep **depot calls** for missing or damaged plants.
think: I expect **paid order work** to continue under mild AI.
I need **verified later income** before reducing either wage.
do: Keep the **paid order queue** and check AI drafts against stock records.
Compare **mortgage and wage figures** with Arun before changing hours.
feel: **Calm** about current wages and an almost-year reserve.
S0.quote: A tidy message cannot tell me whether a tray of seedlings has frozen on a van.
fieldNote: She uses the **AI draft** sometimes but verifies it against real stock.
The near-year **reserve** supports choices without establishing later income.
Her daughters are **family visitors**, not an assumed mortgage resource.

steps.text: Keep paid garden-order calls and check AI drafts against stock records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quicker address correction is welcome as long as the plant actually gets to the right house. I would still call the depot when a delivery is late. A tidy message cannot tell me whether a tray of seedlings has frozen on a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wages should stay steady in this quiet version. Arun and I have nearly a year of expenses saved, and his grounds work brings in a second wage. We have not checked what income would replace either wage if we later chose fewer hours, so I wouldn't make that promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the order queue and continue checking any AI draft against the stock record. This year Arun and I would put the mortgage and actual wages on one sheet before deciding on any shorter rota. In the first year of this mild picture I'd stay in my present paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. We can handle a bad household week without borrowing, and I know how to do this job. I would still rather see the numbers before making later-life plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do you call the depot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer might need the plants for a funeral or a school garden. I don't need a machine to invent a warm paragraph; I need a real arrival date. That's when I ring the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughters be part of a shorter-hours plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We invite our grown daughters for supper, but their wages belong to their homes. We would not add their pay to our mortgage plan. Arun and I would make any hours decision from our own figures.

say: I would ask for **depot evidence** before an AI answer closes a delivery case.
I would request clarity on the **paid case queue**.
think: I could lose **paid order hours** as standard questions move to AI.
I need **real weekly pay** before a nearby counter becomes an option.
do: Compare **twelve existing AI answers** with depot records while taking paid calls.
Ask the supervisor about **paid missing-delivery cases**.
If hours fall, compare **posted nursery rotas** and apply only when real weekly wages/hours after travel cover mortgage and bills.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours, with room to test options.
S1.quote: People will pay for a plant that arrives, not a paragraph saying it might.
fieldNote: Her occasional AI use turns into a **specific comparison** with depot records.
She treats an advertised **counter role** as an option only after actual cuts.
The mortgage makes **weekly pay after travel** more important than a pleasant title.

steps.text: Keep paid order calls and compare twelve AI answers with depot records
Ask supervisor which missing-delivery cases retain paid human hours
After actual hour cuts, compare posted nursery rotas; apply only on mortgage-and-bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that the address bot is useful, but it must not close a missing-delivery case just because it sent a message. I'd ask our supervisor to show us which orders still need a depot call. People will pay for a plant that arrives, not a paragraph saying it might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Standard order questions could leave our queue, and I might lose paid hours. Arun's grounds wage and our savings give us breathing space, but the mortgage still comes every month. There are other local service centres, though their order lines may be changing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare a dozen AI delivery answers with depot records and hand the errors to my supervisor. I'd ask to keep the paid missing-delivery cases that need a person to call the driver. If my hours actually fall over the next few years, I'd compare posted paid nursery-counter work by weekly wages, hours and travel before applying; in the first year I'd keep available shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, but I can test the answers and look nearby. I've learned a new order screen before once colleagues showed me it worked. I don't want to jump jobs on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the order numbers to the supervisor and ask what the paid case queue will be. If the depot record says the van is late, we need to tell the customer that. I would not count an unposted job title as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply for nursery-counter work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the posted rota is real and the complete weekly pay after travel still covers our mortgage and bills. An advertisement for a nice counter is not a wage. I'd keep Fieldgate hours while they are paid.

say: I would warn that **2028 thinking AI** reaches order calls before robots.
I would ask for **honest paid rotas**, not reassuring job titles.
think: I expect a large **Fieldgate call cut** soon after 2028.
I know Arun’s wage and **existing savings** cannot replace mine indefinitely.
do: Check **posted nursery openings** by full-week wages, hours, travel and safe lifting before taking a shift.
Apply if the queue ends in 2028-29; accept only **mortgage-and-bill-covering weekly pay** and hours after travel.
Keep **remaining paid calls** while using bounded existing savings.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss and monthly mortgage pressure.
S2.quote: Nearly a year saved is valuable search time, not an income for the rest of our lives.
fieldNote: She expects her own **call wage** to shrink badly despite a strong reserve.
Arun’s grounds wage is **not enough** alone for their mortgage and bills.
She checks **safe lifting** and real paid hours before a nursery move.

steps.text: Check posted nursery shifts by full-week wages, hours, travel and safe lifting before taking one
Apply if Fieldgate queue ends in 2028-29; accept only mortgage-and-bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel
Keep remaining paid calls while using bounded existing savings for the gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the thinking part of garden orders could be done by cheap AGI by 2028, well before robots arrive around 2031. I would tell coworkers to ask for an honest paid rota instead of assuming the next desk will last. A customer still needs a real delivery, but that may not save my headset job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Fieldgate to cut my calls badly in the first year after 2028. Arun's grounds work may last until later robots, but his wage alone will not cover the mortgage and bills. Nearly a year saved is valuable search time, not an income for the rest of our lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd check posted paid nursery and dispatch-yard openings and list their full-week wages, hours and travel costs. If my Fieldgate queue ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a nursery receiving job with real paid shifts. I would accept only if the weekly wage and hours after travel cover mortgage and bills; otherwise I'd keep any paid calls while we use a bounded part of our existing reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can picture a whole queue gone and the mortgage date still printed in red on our calendar. Savings let me make a plan rather than panic, but I would lose sleep over the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Arun's job cover the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arun would keep his paid grounds shifts while they exist. We would not call his wage enough without checking the actual monthly totals. Robots in 2031 could change his work too, so we won't buy a business on the assumption it is permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a nursery receiving shift involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A nursery receiving shift has plants, trolleys and customers in front of you. I would ask about safe lifting and the posted weekly pay before taking it. I can't treat physical work as guaranteed shelter after 2031.

say: I would favour **paid practical trials** over speculative certificates.
I would say **2034 robots** may also affect physical nursery work.
think: I could test **paid alterations** before 2031 without emptying savings.
I will not count **unpaid favours** as mortgage income.
do: Offer **two fixed-price alterations** and log paid receipts and costs.
Keep **paid Fieldgate shifts** and buy fabric only from receipts; add Saturday alterations after repeat customers pay, keeping a day free.
Apply after 2031 closure only to **posted nursery work** covering mortgage and bills after travel.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test demand before relying on it.
S3.quote: I've mended neighbours' curtains for free, but free favours are not a second wage.
fieldNote: She tests **two paid curtains** before naming alterations an income.
Any extra fabric comes from **actual receipts**, not their reserve.
She keeps **Arun’s paid shifts** in the plan without assuming robot-proof work.

steps.text: Offer two fixed-price curtain alterations and log paid hours and thread costs
Keep paid Fieldgate shifts and buy extra fabric only from alteration receipts
Apply if queue ends in 2031-32 only to posted nursery work with mortgage-and-bill-covering wages/hours after travel
Add Saturday alterations only after repeat paying customers appear; keep one day free with Arun

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to try another kind of work while we still have wages, but not to call it certain. I'd rather learn by taking a real paid shift beside someone than collect a certificate no shop asked for. The nursery's physical work may change when robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could see whether my sewing alterations bring enough paid work to matter before AGI reaches Fieldgate in 2031. I've mended neighbours' curtains for free, but free favours are not a second wage. I still expect fewer order calls, and I won't count hoped-for sewing customers against the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd offer two fixed-price curtain alterations to neighbours and record the hours, thread costs and money actually paid. I'd keep Fieldgate's paid order shifts and use only alteration receipts for any extra fabric. In the first year after 2031, if the queue ends, I'd apply for posted nursery work only if weekly wages and hours after travel cover our mortgage and bills; I'd keep sewing as a small earner if repeat paying customers actually appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the five years would let me test a modest trade without emptying our reserve. I know how to sew; I don't yet know how many neighbours will pay for it. That distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How small is the sewing test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with two curtains, not an online shop and a room full of fabric. If nobody pays, I won't buy stock or tell Arun it is income. If people come back and pay, I'd add a Saturday slot while keeping a day free together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Arun's grounds work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arun would still take grounds shifts while they pay, but neither of us would promise they last beyond 2034 robots. We would keep the mortgage figures in front of us. Our daughters could help carry a curtain, but their money isn't in the plan.

I would say **thinking AI** reaches desk work before later physical robots.
think: I may need **paid hours at sixty-eight** if verified later income is too small.
I will not count **unearned sewing money** against our mortgage.
do: Keep the **paid order queue** and review household income each autumn.
Record **alteration receipts** and count income only after several paid months, less thread and travel; buy no stock from savings.
Apply after 2036 closure only to **paid work** whose full-week wages and hours cover mortgage and bills after travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about unverified later income, with a decade to test demand.
S4.quote: The mortgage is ours, not our daughters'.
fieldNote: She tests **repeat paid demand** before assigning alterations a household role.
Their strong reserve is **finite** and does not establish retirement income.
She excludes adult daughters’ **earnings** from the mortgage plan.

steps.text: Keep paid Fieldgate shifts and review verified later income against mortgage each autumn
Count alteration income after several paid months minus thread/travel; buy no stock from household savings
Apply if queue ends in 2036-37 only to posted mortgage-and-bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family ten years is time to test what people will actually pay for, not a reason to quit a good wage today. Thinking AI may reach Fieldgate orders by 2036, and robots may alter the grounds and nursery work around 2039. I'd make choices from a household ledger, not a prediction on a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still want paid hours at sixty-eight because we have not checked the income that would replace both wages. Almost a year of savings buys choices but won't pay a mortgage forever. If alterations earn repeat money, they may help, but I won't write them in before they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Arun and I would list actual wages, mortgage, bills and any verified later-income figures. I'd keep the paid Fieldgate queue and review alteration receipts every autumn, adding no stock from savings. If the call queue ends in the first year after 2036, I'd apply for posted paid nursery or local service work only if complete weekly wages and hours after travel cover our bills; if later income falls short I'd keep paid work in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the decade gives us time to check the numbers. I am not ready to promise a retirement birthday. I'd be relieved if the sewing stays a small paid pleasure rather than having to carry our whole house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you know whether alterations count as income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count it only after several paid months, with thread and travel costs taken out. Two neighbours being kind is not a business forecast. I might keep doing alterations on Saturdays even if Fieldgate calls continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your daughters to help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is ours, not our daughters'. We would show them the plan if they asked, but we would not make their earnings part of it. If we need wages at sixty-eight, we will look for work we can still do safely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I could lose my Fieldgate wage before another paid week is ready. It would help to see posted rotas with real wages and hours, and to know which nurseries have work that can be done safely. Our savings give us time, but I wouldn't put the daughters' pay into the plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask which work still has a customer at the end of it. A plant delivered on Tuesday is worth more than a perfect message sent on Monday. I would like the person who fixes that delivery to have paid hours.

headlineQuote: A plant delivered on Tuesday is worth more than a perfect message sent on Monday.
portrait: Zoe is a **58-year-old** experienced garden-order agent with secondary school education.
She earns **higher pay**, has nearly a year saved and still pays a mortgage.
She uses AI **occasionally** and checks drafts against stock and depot records.
She tests **paid alterations** modestly while keeping the call wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when the order queue might end before another paid week is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Posted rotas** showing real wages, hours and safe nursery duties.
